q: Which structure is 4-ethyl-2,2,5-trimethylheptane?
h: Draw a seven-carbon chain, number it, and place the groups. Then check each choice: find its longest chain and number it from the end nearer the first branch.
w: Heptane is a seven-carbon chain. C2 carries two methyls, C4 an ethyl and C5 a methyl. In the structure with a tert-butyl end, one CH2, then CH(CH2CH3), then CH(CH3) followed by an ethyl end, the longest chain has seven carbons, and numbering from the tert-butyl end gives locants 2,2,4,5 (the other direction gives 3,4,6,6). Of the others, one swaps the ethyl and methyl positions, one moves the gem-dimethyl to C3, and one has only a six-carbon parent chain.
x: Here the methyl is on C4 and the ethyl on C5: this is 5-ethyl-2,2,4-trimethylheptane.
The two methyls sit on C3, not C2. Numbered properly this is 4-ethyl-3,3,5-trimethylheptane.
The chain ends in an isopropyl group, so the longest chain has only six carbons: 4-ethyl-2,2,5-trimethylhexane.

q: Which condensed formula is 2-bromo-4-methylhexane?
h: Write a six-carbon chain and number it. Put Br on C2 and CH<sub>3</sub> on C4, then name each choice yourself, numbering from the end nearer the first substituent.
w: Hexane is a six-carbon chain; the halogen is named as a prefix (bromo) and listed alphabetically with the alkyl group. Placing Br on C2 and a methyl on C4 gives CH3–CHBr–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH3. Numbered from the other end the locants would be 3 and 5, so 2,4 is the correct numbering: CH3CHBrCH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3.
x: Here the methyl is on C2 and Br on C4 (numbering from the end nearer the first substituent): 4-bromo-2-methylhexane. The two substituents have traded places.
Br and CH<sub>3</sub> are on adjacent carbons C3 and C4: 3-bromo-4-methylhexane.
Br and CH<sub>3</sub> are on adjacent carbons C2 and C3: 2-bromo-3-methylhexane. The methyl must be two carbons away from the C–Br carbon.

q: Which structure is 4-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene?
h: In a cycloalkene, C1 and C2 are the alkene carbons. Number through the double bond in the direction that gives the substituents the lowest locants.
w: The double bond is between C1 and C2, and C1 carries the methyl. Continue around the ring from C2: C3, then C4 carries Cl. The ring with the methyl on an alkene carbon and Cl on the carbon directly across the ring from it (1,4) is the answer. Of the others, one has Cl at C3 (3-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene), one is 5-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene, and one swaps Cl and CH3 (1-chloro-4-methylcyclohexene).
x: Here Cl is on the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon right next to the alkene: 3-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene.
Numbering through the double bond from the methyl carbon, Cl lands on C5 (the other direction gives 2,4, which loses at the first locant). This is 5-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene.
The chlorine is on the alkene carbon and the methyl is at C4: this is 1-chloro-4-methylcyclohexene.

q: Haloperidol, an antipsychotic drug, is shown. Which choice correctly describes its functional groups?
c: a ketone, a tertiary alcohol, a tertiary amine and two aryl halides
a ketone, a secondary alcohol, a tertiary amine and two aryl halides
a ketone, a tertiary alcohol, a secondary amine and two aryl halides
a ketone, a tertiary alcohol, a tertiary amine and two tertiary alkyl halides
h: Classify an alcohol by the carbons on the C–OH carbon, an amine by the carbons on N, and a halide by the kind of carbon bearing it.
w: The C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons (the aryl ring and a CH2), so it is a ketone. The OH carbon in the piperidine ring is bonded to three carbons (two ring CH2 groups and the aryl ring), so the alcohol is tertiary. The ring nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (two ring carbons and the side chain), so the amine is tertiary. F and Cl are bonded directly to benzene carbons, so they are aryl halides. Answer: a ketone, a tertiary alcohol, a tertiary amine and two aryl halides.
x: The C–OH carbon has no H: it is bonded to two ring carbons and the chlorophenyl ring, which makes the alcohol tertiary.
The piperidine N has no N–H; its three bonds all go to carbon, so the amine is tertiary.
Both halogens are on sp<sup>2</sup> benzene carbons, which makes them aryl halides; a tertiary alkyl halide has X on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon bonded to three carbons.

q: Which compound contains both a lactone and a tertiary amine?
h: A lactone is a cyclic ester: the ring contains O bonded to a C=O. A tertiary amine N carries three carbons and no H.
w: The five-membered ring with O–C(=O) in the ring and a CH2N(CH3)2 side chain has both: the ring oxygen bonded to the carbonyl carbon makes a cyclic ester (lactone), and the N bonded to three carbons is a tertiary amine. One distractor has a secondary amine (N–H), one has an N–H in the ring next to C=O (a lactam, a cyclic amide), and one has a ring ether with a ketone carbon that is not bonded to the ring oxygen.
x: The lactone is right, but the side-chain N carries an H and only two carbons, so it is a secondary amine.
The ring contains N–C(=O), which is a lactam (cyclic amide), not a lactone.
In this ring the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone; the ring oxygen is an ether, not part of an ester.

q: Menthol, the cooling compound in mint, is shown. How many tertiary (3°) carbons does it contain? (A tertiary carbon is bonded to exactly three other carbons.)
h: Go carbon by carbon and count carbon neighbors only; the O of the OH does not count.
w: Count C–C bonds at each branch point. The isopropyl CH is bonded to two methyls and a ring carbon (3°). The ring carbon carrying the isopropyl group is bonded to two ring carbons and the isopropyl carbon (3°). The ring carbon carrying the methyl is bonded to two ring carbons and the methyl (3°). The C–OH carbon is bonded to only two carbons (plus O), so it is secondary. Answer: 3.
x: This misses the isopropyl CH, which is bonded to two CH<sub>3</sub> groups and to the ring: three carbons.
This counts the C–OH carbon. It is bonded to only two carbons; the oxygen does not make it tertiary.
Each branching ring carbon also counts; only one of the three tertiary carbons is in the isopropyl group.

q: The artificial sweetener aspartame is shown. Which functional group is NOT present?
h: Look at every C=O and name it by what is bonded to the carbonyl carbon.
w: Aspartame has three C=O groups. One carbonyl carbon is bonded to OCH3 (a methyl ester), one is bonded to N–H (an amide, the peptide bond), and one is bonded to OH (a carboxylic acid). It also has a primary amine and a benzene ring. No carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbons, so there is no ketone.
x: The C(=O)OCH<sub>3</sub> group at the phenylalanine end is a methyl ester.
The C(=O)–NH linking the two amino acids is an amide (peptide bond).
The CH<sub>2</sub>C(=O)OH side chain is a carboxylic acid.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The OH is the principal group: it gets the suffix and the lowest possible locant, even if that gives the C=C a higher number.
w: The six-carbon chain contains the OH, the C=C and the Cl. The alcohol is the highest-priority group, so it is named with the suffix -ol and must get the lowest locant. Numbering from the CH3 end puts OH on C2 (from the other end it would be C5). Then Cl is on C4 and the double bond starts at C5. Name: 4-chlorohex-5-en-2-ol.
x: This numbers from the alkene end. The OH outranks the C=C, so the OH (not the alkene) gets the lower locant.
When an alcohol is present, it must be the suffix (-ol); using the prefix hydroxy- here breaks the principal-group rule.
Counting from the CH<sub>3</sub> end, the Cl carbon is C4 (C2 carries OH, C3 is CH<sub>2</sub>), not C3.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: The carbon bearing OH is C1. Go around the ring in the direction that reaches a methyl soonest.
w: The OH carbon is C1. Going toward the adjacent methyl puts the methyls at C2 and C4; the other direction gives C4 and C6. The set {2,4} is lower, so the name is 2,4-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol.
x: This goes around the ring the wrong way; {2,4} is lower than {4,6} at the first point of difference.
An OH principal group is named as the suffix -ol on the parent (cyclohexanol), not as a hydroxy prefix.
3,5-Dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol would have no methyl on a carbon next to C1. Here one methyl sits on the carbon directly beside the C–OH carbon, so the locants are 2 and 4.

q: Which structure is N,2-dimethylbutan-1-amine?
h: The locant N means the group is on nitrogen; a number means it is on that carbon of the chain. C1 is the carbon bonded to N.
w: Butan-1-amine has N on C1 of a four-carbon chain. 2-Methyl places a methyl on C2, and N-methyl places a methyl on the nitrogen. The compound CH3NH–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2CH3 fits. The others put the carbon methyl on C3, put both methyls on nitrogen, or put both methyls on C2 with no N-methyl.
x: Here the C-methyl is on C3 (third carbon from N): N,3-dimethylbutan-1-amine.
Both methyls are on nitrogen: N,N-dimethylbutan-1-amine, a tertiary amine.
This is a primary amine with two methyls on C2: 2,2-dimethylbutan-1-amine; it has no N-methyl group.

q:
Which statements about the compound shown are correct?
I. The alcohol is secondary.
II. The amine is secondary.
III. The chlorine is bonded to a primary carbon.
h: Alcohols and halides are classified by the carbon that bears the OH or X; amines by how many carbons are bonded to N.
w: I is true: the C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons (CH3 and CH2), so the alcohol is secondary. II is false: the nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (the CH2 on each side and a CH3) and has no N–H, so it is a tertiary amine. III is true: the C–Cl carbon is bonded to only one other carbon, so it is a primary alkyl chloride. Answer: I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: the CH<sub>2</sub>Cl carbon is attached to just one carbon, so it is primary.
Statement II is false: amines are classified by the number of carbons on nitrogen, and this N has three, so it is tertiary.
Statement I is also true: the carbinol carbon carries a CH<sub>3</sub> and a CH<sub>2</sub>, two carbons, so the alcohol is secondary.

q: Which intermolecular forces act between molecules in pure liquid triethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N?
c: dispersion, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonding
hydrogen bonding and dispersion forces only
h: To donate a hydrogen bond, a molecule needs H bonded directly to N, O or F.
w: All molecules have dispersion forces. Triethylamine is a pyramidal molecule with polar C–N bonds and a lone pair, so it has a net dipole and shows dipole–dipole attractions. It has no N–H bond, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other (the N can only accept an H bond from a donor such as water). Answer: dispersion and dipole–dipole forces only.
x: The pyramidal N with a lone pair gives triethylamine a net dipole moment, so dipole–dipole forces are also present.
Hydrogen bonding between molecules of the pure amine needs an N–H donor; a tertiary amine has none.
A tertiary amine has no N–H, so there is no hydrogen bonding in the pure liquid; its permanent dipole gives dipole–dipole forces instead.

q:
Which of these compounds can form hydrogen bonds between molecules of the same compound in the pure liquid?
I. ethyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2CH3
II. propanamide, CH3CH2CONH2
III. methylamine, CH3NH2
h: A pure liquid can hydrogen-bond to itself only if its molecules have both an acceptor (lone pair on N, O, F) and a donor (H on N, O or F).
w: I is false: ethyl acetate has O acceptors but every H is on carbon, so it has no donor. II is true: the amide NH2 donates and the C=O oxygen accepts, so amides hydrogen-bond strongly. III is true: methylamine has N–H donors and an N lone pair acceptor. Answer: II and III only.
x: Statement III is misjudged: methylamine has two N–H bonds and a lone pair, so it is both donor and acceptor.
Statement II is misjudged: the NH<sub>2</sub> of a primary amide is a good donor and the C=O is a good acceptor.
Statement I is misjudged: an ester can accept hydrogen bonds (from water, for example) but has no O–H or N–H to donate, so it cannot hydrogen-bond to itself.

q: These three isomeric amines (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>9</sub>N) have the same molar mass. Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Count N–H bonds in each isomer, then consider how compact each molecule is.
w: Primary amine I (propan-1-amine) has two N–H donors and the most surface area, so it boils highest (48 °C). Secondary amine II (N-methylethanamine) has one N–H, so it forms fewer hydrogen bonds (36 °C). Tertiary amine III (trimethylamine) has no N–H and cannot hydrogen-bond to itself; it is also the most compact, so it boils far lower (3 °C). Ranking: III < II < I.
x: This is the reverse order. More N–H bonds mean more hydrogen bonding and a higher boiling point, so the primary amine is highest.
Trimethylamine has no N–H and cannot hydrogen-bond to itself, so it must have the lowest boiling point, not a middle one.
The primary amine has two N–H donors versus one for II, so I boils higher than II.

q: Which compound has the highest boiling point?
h: Molar mass matters, but the number of O–H groups per molecule matters more when the masses are similar.
w: Propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) (92 g/mol) has three O–H groups, so each molecule forms a dense network of hydrogen bonds; it boils near 290 °C. Ethane-1,2-diol (62 g/mol, two OH) boils at 197 °C, hexan-1-ol (102 g/mol, one OH) at 157 °C, and heptane (100 g/mol, dispersion forces only) at 98 °C.
x: Hexan-1-ol is the heaviest alcohol here, but with only one O–H it forms far fewer hydrogen bonds than glycerol (157 °C vs about 290 °C).
Heptane has the largest molar mass but only dispersion forces, so it boils lowest of the four.
Ethane-1,2-diol has two O–H groups and boils high (197 °C), but glycerol has three and a larger mass.

q: Which compound is least soluble in hexane?
h: Like dissolves like: hexane offers only dispersion forces.
w: Hexane is nonpolar and attracts solutes only by dispersion forces. To dissolve in it, a compound must give up its own attractions. Ethane-1,2-diol is held together by strong hydrogen bonds from two OH groups per molecule, and hexane cannot replace them, so the two liquids are nearly immiscible. Diethyl ether, toluene and 1-chlorobutane are mostly hydrocarbon and mix freely with hexane.
x: Diethyl ether has a small dipole and no O–H; its two ethyl groups make it fully miscible with hexane.
Toluene is a nonpolar hydrocarbon held together by dispersion forces, just like hexane, so it mixes freely.
1-Chlorobutane is only weakly polar and has no hydrogen bonding, so it dissolves readily in hexane.

q: Dodecan-1-amine, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>11</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, is insoluble in water but dissolves in dilute aqueous HCl. What is the best explanation?
c: HCl converts it to an alkylammonium chloride, whose ions are held in water by ion–dipole forces
HCl breaks the hydrogen bonds between amine molecules, freeing them to hydrogen-bond with water
HCl adds Cl to the alkyl chain, making the chain polar enough to dissolve
HCl converts the amine into an amide, which hydrogen-bonds strongly to water
h: What does an amine do with a strong acid? Compare a neutral molecule and an ion in water.
w: An amine is a base. HCl protonates the nitrogen to give CH3(CH2)11NH3+ Cl−, an ionic salt. Water molecules orient their partial charges around the ions; these ion–dipole attractions are much stronger than the hydrogen bonds the neutral amine can make, and they pull the long chain into solution. Answer: it becomes an alkylammonium chloride held in water by ion–dipole forces. Basifying the solution with NaOH would bring the neutral amine back out.
x: The neutral amine already can hydrogen-bond with water through its NH<sub>2</sub>; the C<sub>12</sub> chain is what keeps it insoluble. Only forming an ion changes that.
HCl does not react with a saturated alkyl chain; it reacts with the basic nitrogen lone pair.
An amide needs a carbonyl group; HCl only protonates the amine, giving an ammonium salt.

q: These three compounds have nearly the same molar mass (72–74 g/mol). Rank them from least to most soluble in water.
h: Neither ether can donate a hydrogen bond, but both can accept one from water. Which oxygen is easier for water to reach?
w: Pentane (I) has no polar group and is almost insoluble (about 0.04 g/L). Diethyl ether (II) can accept hydrogen bonds from water at its oxygen, so it dissolves moderately (about 69 g/L). Tetrahydrofuran (III) has the same C4O composition, but its alkyl groups are tied back into a ring, so the oxygen lone pairs are exposed and less shielded by flexible ethyl groups; THF is miscible with water in all proportions. Ranking: I < II < III.
x: THF is more soluble than diethyl ether: tying the carbons into a ring leaves its oxygen more exposed for hydrogen bonds from water.
Pentane has no way to interact with water except weak dispersion forces, so it is the least soluble, below diethyl ether.
This is the reverse order; the hydrocarbon is least soluble and the cyclic ether is most soluble.

q: 2-Nitrophenol boils at about 216 °C, while its isomer 4-nitrophenol boils at about 279 °C. What is the best explanation?
c: The O–H of 2-nitrophenol hydrogen-bonds to its own nitro group, so it forms fewer hydrogen bonds to other molecules
4-Nitrophenol has a larger molar mass, so its dispersion forces are stronger
2-Nitrophenol has no net dipole moment because its two groups are next to each other
The nitro group of 4-nitrophenol makes its O–H a weaker acid, so it hydrogen-bonds more strongly
h: The two isomers have the same atoms and the same groups. Look at how close the OH is to the nitro oxygens in each.
w: In 2-nitrophenol the OH and NO2 are on adjacent carbons, so the O–H forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond to a nitro oxygen (a six-membered ring). That H is then mostly unavailable for hydrogen bonds to neighboring molecules. In 4-nitrophenol the groups are too far apart, so each O–H hydrogen-bonds to other molecules, which raises the boiling point. Answer: 2-nitrophenol forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond, leaving fewer intermolecular hydrogen bonds. (The same effect lets 2-nitrophenol be separated from the 4-isomer by steam distillation.)
x: They are isomers (both C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>, 139 g/mol), so molar mass cannot explain the difference.
Ortho-disubstituted benzenes with polar groups do have net dipoles; the OH and NO<sub>2</sub> dipoles do not cancel.
A para nitro group makes the phenol more acidic, not less; and acidity is not what sets the boiling point here.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Choose a parent chain that contains both C=C bonds, then number to give the double bonds the lowest locants.
w: The longest chain that includes both double bonds has six carbons (it runs from the =CH2 to one of the methyls on the far alkene carbon). Numbering from the =CH2 end gives the double bonds locants 1 and 4 (the other direction gives 2 and 5). The methyls are then on C3 and C5: 3,5-dimethylhexa-1,4-diene.
x: This numbers from the wrong end. The double bonds must get the lowest locants: {1,4} beats {2,5}.
The parent chain must contain both double bonds when possible. Treating the vinyl group as a substituent leaves one alkene out of the chain.
The chain has six carbons, not seven: the far alkene carbon carries two methyls, and only one of them is part of the chain.
